opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those questions where it's really easy to slide from a behavioral observation to a representational claim without noticing you've done it. So the fact that a network can reverse a list, even reverse lists longer than the ones it saw in training, tells you something about the function it has learned. It doesn't, by itself, tell you that inside the network there's something that looks like a symbolic data structure with discrete slots and a pointer walking backwards through them.

The way I think about it is that there's a hierarchy of claims you might make. The weakest is: the input–output behavior is consistent with a symbolic algorithm. A stronger claim is: the network's internal states can be decoded into the variables that algorithm would use. Say you can linearly read out "position in the sequence" and "identity of the element at that position." And the strongest claim is that those representations are causally implicated in the way the algorithm says they should be, so if you intervene on the representation of position, the output changes exactly as a symbolic account predicts. A lot of the classic debate between connectionists and people in the Fodor and Pylyshyn tradition was conducted mostly at that first level, and I think the field has gotten more interesting now that we have tools to actually probe the second and third.

What you often find in practice is something in between. The network has representations that are approximately symbolic. They have roughly the right compositional structure, and roles and fillers are somewhat separable. But they're also graded and context-sensitive in ways a pure symbol system wouldn't be. And those deviations are often exactly where the model breaks down: much longer lists, repeated elements, distributions it hasn't seen. So I'd say the success at reversal and the partial symbolic structure are two sides of the same coin, and the places where the structure isn't fully symbolic predict the generalization failures.

For me the upshot is that "does the network have symbols?" isn't really a yes-or-no question. It's more useful to ask to what degree the representations implement the abstractions a symbolic theory posits, and whether that degree is enough to get humanlike generalization. That's also why I care so much about evaluating on out-of-distribution cases. In-distribution accuracy can't distinguish a network that has learned the abstract operation from one that has learned a very good approximation that happens to cover the training range.

r001.rationale: The response says list reversal alone does not establish symbolic internal structure. It describes approximate symbolic representations separately, but does not clearly state that the reversal ability implies they reflect the lists’ symbolic structure.

r002.rationale: It describes checking whether internal states can be decoded into algorithmic variables, including reading out sequence position and element identity—an equivalent way to map hypothesized structure onto vector representations.

r003.rationale: The response makes a general claim about what networks often exhibit, but does not report that Linzen and his collaborators found a close structural correspondence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think list reversal is a nice case precisely because it looks trivial and turns out to be diagnostic. If you ask a person to reverse a sequence they've never seen before, they'll just do it, regardless of length or of which tokens happen to be in it. That's because they have a procedure that treats the elements as variables: take the last thing, then the thing before it, and so on. The identity of the items doesn't matter and the length doesn't matter beyond memory limits. That's what I'd call a symbolic solution. The question for a neural network is whether, when it succeeds at reversal, it has arrived at something like that, or whether it's learned a large collection of more local associations that happen to cover the training distribution.

The way you tell those apart is generalization. If you train on sequences up to length ten and the model falls apart at length twelve, or it works on lengths it has seen but fails when you introduce a token that never appeared in a particular position during training, that tells you the internal representation isn't really encoding "position k maps to position n minus k" as an abstract relation. It's encoding something more like a lookup over specific configurations. And historically that's what we saw with a lot of recurrent models and even early transformers: good in-distribution performance, with length generalization that was fragile in ways that are hard to square with a genuinely compositional solution.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think the right framing is "either the network has symbols or it doesn't." The interesting work, including some of the mechanistic interpretability results on small transformers, suggests that networks can learn circuits that are functionally quite close to a symbolic algorithm. You can find attention heads that effectively implement an index-to-index mapping. But those circuits are often entangled with surface statistics, and they can be approximate in ways that only show up under distribution shift. So I think of the relationship as something like: reversal is a probe for whether the model has induced variables and operations over them, and the answer tends to be "partly, and in ways that depend heavily on the architecture and the training data."

What I find most useful about this is that it connects to the bigger question about language. Reversal is a toy, but the structure it requires, binding items to positions and operating over that binding, is the same thing you need for agreement across an embedded clause or for interpreting a relative clause. If a model can't get reversal right in a robust way, I'm skeptical that its apparent syntactic competence is built on the kind of representations we'd want. And conversely, when we do see robust generalization, that's evidence that whatever is going on inside, even if it's distributed and messy, is doing the work that symbols do in our theories.

r001.rationale: The response says robust generalization can be evidence of symbol-like processing, but says reversal success may instead come from local associations. It does not state that the ability to reverse lists itself implies implicitly symbolic representations.

r002.rationale: It discusses using generalization to distinguish algorithms from local associations and mentions attention heads, but does not describe mapping a hypothesized symbolic structure onto the network’s internal vector representations.

r003.rationale: It mentions some mechanistic interpretability findings about circuits approximating symbolic algorithms, but does not report that Linzen and collaborators found a close structural correspondence between hypothesized list representations and internal vector representations.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the computation a system performs from the representations it uses to perform it. Reversing a list has a very natural symbolic description: you have a sequence of elements, and you return those same elements in the opposite order. But a neural network succeeding at that task doesn’t, by itself, tell us that it represents the elements and their positions in a symbolic way.

It might have learned a procedure that generalizes to arbitrary elements and arbitrary lengths, or it might have learned something that works only within the range of examples it was trained on. Those can look very similar on a particular test set. So I’d want to ask: What happens with longer lists? What happens with unfamiliar elements? And can we intervene on the internal representations to establish how the network is doing the task?

Systematic generalization would be evidence for a more abstract procedure, but even then, the behavioral result doesn’t uniquely determine the internal mechanism. That’s something we have to investigate rather than infer just from the fact that the network can reverse a list.

r001.rationale: The response says list reversal alone does not show that the network represents elements and positions symbolically, and that behavior does not determine the internal mechanism.

r002.rationale: It proposes intervening on internal representations but does not describe mapping a hypothesized symbolic structure onto the network’s vector representations.

r003.rationale: The response reports no finding by Linzen and collaborators about a structural correspondence; it says the internal mechanism requires investigation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish the behavior from the mechanism. Reversing a list is something we can describe with a very simple symbolic algorithm: take the last element, put it first, and keep going. But the fact that a neural network produces the right answer doesn’t tell us that it’s implementing that algorithm, or that its internal representations are symbolic.

One question is how systematically it generalizes. If it’s trained on short lists, can it reverse much longer lists? Can it handle elements it hasn’t seen in those positions? That would provide evidence that it has learned something more general than patterns specific to the training examples. But even then, we’d want to look inside the network and test hypotheses about the mechanism, ideally by intervening on its representations.

So I wouldn’t say that success on list reversal establishes symbolic structure. It gives us a useful setting in which to ask what kinds of representations and computations support systematic behavior, and whether those resemble the symbolic algorithm we would write down.

r001.rationale: The candidate says successful reversal does not establish symbolic internal structure, directly rejecting the criterion’s implication.

r002.rationale: It proposes inspecting and intervening on representations, but does not describe mapping a hypothesized symbolic structure onto internal vector representations.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not report a finding by Linzen and collaborators or a close correspondence between symbolic and vector representations.
